The transcript will be multiple pages in length; how long depends on the length of the conversation.

Supplied input:
**Input Sections**

**Transcript:**

What do you do when you can feel the machinations of the music industry wearing you down? It’s a question that the four members of FIZZ found themselves asking themselves, and each other, as each struggled with the day-to-day grind of keeping their heads above water as solo artists. It wasn’t a feeing born out of a lack of individual success, either, something that each of them have tasted; in 2021, dodie’s debut album went to number three on the UK charts, after a rise to prominence on YouTube that saw her rack up hundreds of millions of views. Orla Gartland’s first album, also released two years ago, made the top ten, too, and met with rave reviews.

Greta Isaac and Martin Luke Brown, meanwhile, have made their own solo waves, the former with a searingly experimental blend of folk and pop and the latter as a singer-songwriter who trades in witty, thoughtful confessionals. Back in June, the four of them revealed themselves to comprise FIZZ, after having initially shrouded their identity in mystery. Their debut album, The Secret to Life, is their answer to the conundrum of how to preserve passion for making art in an unforgiving climate; as they explained to us, the key is to have a laugh with your mates.

Would it have been possible to make a record like this if you weren’t all such good friends to begin with?

Orla Gartland: I think so. We’ve known each other for eight, nine, ten years, and collaborated in different ways; backing vocals on each other’s songs, and I’ve played in dodie’s live band. So, there’s a bedrock there that has helped us fast-track so much of this band. There’s a deep knowing of each other, collectively and individually, and I think the band wouldn’t have come together so quickly without that.

dodie:After lockdown, Greta and Martin moved into this flat with me, and Orla lives just down the road, so we found ourselves hanging out a lot more, and eventually we ended up going out to this studio called Middle Farm in South Devon, where Orla was doing live sessions for her album. It’s run by this production wizard called Pete Miles, who very much encourages people to be themselves musically, and in their lives too. We all worked together there and it felt amazing, like a little taste of escape. It does feel as if the band was destined to be.

Had you all reached a point with your own careers where it felt as if there was something you wanted to escape from? 

Martin Luke Brown: 100%, yeah. We made the record over two separate weeks at Middle Farm, the first one being in December of 2021, and I remember saying just before we headed down there the first time, I just wanted a holiday from the reality of what its is to be a musician. It had become very jobbing for me. I love music so, so much, and it’s such a big, expansive thing, but you create your own box to live in and it felt like such a shame that I was stuck in such a narrow little lane. I think we all felt that way a little bit, and there was this unspoken thing of us all wanting to invert how we’d been doing things for the last ten years, and just go back to being 12-year-olds in the garage, hashing it out and having a laugh. And that’s exactly what happened. If anything, it’s gotten a bit out of hand! We weren’t expecting to sign a record deal. 

dodie: We’re all very proud of what we’ve done, but I think we wanted to break free from the shackles of what’s expected from us and, also, the pressure we put on ourselves, as well. It was a chance to get away from our own egos and get together as friends, with no expectations.

Greta Isaac: And Middle Farm is a very egoless place; you change your own bedsheets, you cook your own food, you sit around the dinner table every night whether you feel like it or not, and you discuss how you’re feeling. It’s not a results-oriented place at all. Pete is about setting things up as a bit of a playground for you to experiment and then capturing it on tape. That was so refreshing to us coming from London, where it feels like a bit of a treadmill, where you find yourself hunched over a laptop agonising over snare sounds.

Was it important to feel like you could play around with ideas and just follow your noses creatively? 

Brown: I know I can be guilty, with my own stuff, of starting out with something amazing and then agonising over it, relentlessly trying to improve on it and perfect it, and all I end up doing is sucking the soul out of it. We were really firm on not allowing that to happen, and letting this be whatever it is. 

Isaac: What I found very quickly making this album is that between our friendship and our musical ability, that was enough. It didn’t need to be overthought or analysed; it was a bit like a dream, going in, coming out and only realising what we had once we were finished. 

Gartland: It took me until after we’d put twelve songs on a playlist for me to make sense of what we’d made, because it all happened so fast. We didn’t allow ourselves to mess with it after a certain point for the good of the music, which is nice, because now it’s like a time capsule of that moment in our lives.

Brown: I like the idea that it’s going to bring back a load of memories, listening to it when we’re 50 or 60 years old. That’s what we’ll focus on then, not whether the snare sound is exactly right or whether we made a mistake somewhere.

When you were thinking about musical references for the record, was a sense of fun the most important thing? 

Isaac: I think the album speaks to what we were craving, not only in our own projects but in music in general. There’s a theatricality to it that goes back tot the seventies and eighties, referencing bands like Queen and Jellyfish, like a high camp to it. That’s something The Last Dinner Party do really well, too, to have this kind of uncompromising grandeur in the way they present music to people. That’s really rare these days. 

Brown: It doesn’t feel very Brit, does it? It feels like in this country you have to be very self-effacing, and take up as little room as possible, and be humble and say, “here’s my silly little songs”. Whereas there’s tracks on this album with five key changes! 

Gartland: It’s not an album that apologises for itself in any way. That comes from the group mentality where, in our own projects, we might be a little bit more timid but, when there’s safety in number, why not make the songs the loudest, most arrogant versions of themselves? 

dodie: And that’s being reflected in the way that we’re presenting it now, visually, which is just uncompromisingly loud. I love when people are proud of the work that they make and don’t apologise for it.

There’s a real mix of songs that are lyrically playful on the record – like ‘Rocket League’ – and tracks that are more thoughtful and vulnerable. How do you go about balancing that?

Brown: Me and Gret have got probably fifty voice notes of songs like ‘Rocket League’. We could have a whole album full of one-minute songs about everyday nonsense. That one started out as the others just having a laugh about me playing Rocket League all the time, and it’s not something I would ever have made into a song myself, but it’s so ridiculous and silly and it encapsulates what we’re about quite nicely. 

dodie: The beauty of it being an escape for us is that we didn’t want the album to be too careful or considered; it was just supposed to be about exploring our friendship. And ironically, that’s what’s ended up being the overarching theme, which is that the secret to life is experiencing all that life has to offer with your friends by your side. 

Isaac: I feel like only ten years’ worth of friendship can allow for that spectrum of pure, unadulterated silliness, from being goofy to transitioning to more sincere songs like ‘Close One’, ‘As Good As It Gets’ and ‘You, Me, Lonely’, that comes from feeling safe enough to be vulnerable, among people who feel like your family. That was really true at Middle Farm. We’d be crying one minute and cackling with laughter the next.

How does it feel to be finally playing these songs live after sitting on them for a while? 

Isaac: We’re all huge fans of each other, but I think when you get to know people so intimately, when you’re having breakfast together every day, or going out for a walk and getting coffee, or having an argument about something – all these everyday things – it’s really easy to forget how talented everybody is. I look over at Orla fucking shredding on the guitar and think, “oh my god! I forgot you play guitar. You were in my flat three hours ago.”

Gartland: There’s something really special about that; just looking around you and being proud of your mates.

a) Gather relevant information about the client through interviews, assessments, and/or collateral sources. b) Review and analyze the collected data, including the client's presenting problems, symptoms, and history. c) Identify potential diagnoses, if applicable, based on diagnostic criteria and clinical judgment. d) Develop a comprehensive case formulation by integrating psychological theories, understanding the underlying factors contributing to the client's difficulties. e) Present the case formulation in a clear and concise manner, capturing the interplay between various psychological factors and providing a holistic understanding.

Input specification:
* In-Depth Client Interviews: Report from interviews with the client, focusing on their current concerns, mental health history, personal background, and life experiences. Explore their emotional, behavioral, and cognitive aspects to gain a full perspective. * Comprehensive Assessments: Results from psychological assessments, such as personality tests, cognitive evaluations, and symptom checklists, to measure various aspects of the client's psychological functioning. * Collateral Information: Additional information from secondary sources like family members, previous therapists, medical records, and educational or occupational reports to complement and verify the client's self-reported information. * Symptom and Pattern Analysis: Symptoms and behavioral patterns over time. Pay attention to how symptoms manifest, their severity, frequency, and triggers. Consider both current and past symptoms in the context of the client's life circumstances.

Supplied input:
**Input Sections**

**In-Depth Client Interviews:**

* Client reports experiencing persistent and intense sadness, loss of interest in activities, feelings of worthlessness, and difficulty concentrating for the past several months.
* Client discloses a history of childhood trauma, including emotional and physical abuse.
* Client expresses difficulty regulating emotions and forming close relationships.

**Comprehensive Assessments:**

* Beck Depression Inventory (BDI-II) score: 45 (severe depression)
* Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI-2) profile: Elevated scores on scales measuring depression, anxiety, and emotional dysregulation.
* Cognitive assessment: Deficits in attention and memory.

**Collateral Information:**

* Family members confirm client's history of childhood trauma.
* Previous therapist's notes indicate a previous diagnosis of major depressive disorder.
* Medical records show no significant physical health concerns.

**Symptom and Pattern Analysis:**

* Persistent and severe depressive symptoms for over two months.
* History of childhood trauma and emotional dysregulation.
* Cognitive deficits in attention and memory.
requested_output_constraints: * Collected Data: Integrate all gathered data, including interview insights, assessment results, and collateral information, to form a coherent picture of the client's psychological state. * Diagnosis Identification: Using the DSM-5 or other diagnostic tools, identify potential diagnoses. Document how the client's symptoms align with diagnostic criteria, considering differential diagnoses and comorbid conditions. * Case Formulation Development: Develop a case formulation that integrates psychological theories, diagnostic findings, and an understanding of the underlying factors contributing to the client's difficulties. This should reflect the complexity of the client's psychological profile and provide insight into their mental health condition. * Case Formulation: Present the case formulation in a manner that captures the interplay between various psychological factors. Ensure it provides a holistic understanding of the client's issues, considering both the individual and their environment. This presentation should be accessible to both the client and other professionals, as necessary.

- Case formulation should consider multiple dimensions, including biological, psychological, contextual, and cultural factors.  - Utilize evidence-based psychological theories and models to guide the formulation process.  - Ensure ethical considerations, confidentiality, and privacy of the client's information.  - Collaboration and consultation with colleagues can enhance the quality and accuracy of the case formulation.  - Best practices include regularly reviewing and updating the case formulation as new information becomes available.

prompt_text:
Task objective:
Developing a field report after a study

Task procedure/context:
A field report is written after a study to explain a study. It is broken into sections and often includes the wider implications

Input specification:
* Introduction: A few sentences. Notes on the study. * Findings: Notes/a few sentences. Results from the study. * Conclusion: Notes/a few sentences. Key findings and links to intro.

Supplied input:
**Input Sections**

**Introduction:**

The study focused on assessing the impacts of urbanization on flood discharge and frequency across various urban and rural stream basins in the United States. Conducted by the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), the research aimed to study the consequences of land-use changes, particularly the transition from natural landscapes to urban settings with extensive impervious surfaces, on hydrological responses during rainfall and snowmelt events. The study involved:
* Comparative analysis of hydrological data from multiple urban and rural stream basins.
* Evaluation of changes in peak discharge rates and flood frequencies pre- and post-urbanization.
* Investigation of urban infrastructure factors, such as bridges, culverts, and vegetation removal, on water flow and stability of stream banks.

**Findings:**

Main findings include:
* A significant increase in the size and frequency of flood events in urbanized areas, attributed to reduced natural water storage capacity and faster runoff rates.
* Specific increases in peak discharge rates ranging from 100% to 600% for 2-year flood events and 20% to 300% for 10-year flood events in urban areas compared to their rural counterparts.
* Identification of factors like infrastructure constriction and vegetation removal that further intensify urban flooding risks.

**Conclusion:**

The study concludes that urbanization significantly elevates flood discharge rates and frequencies, posing risks to urban communities. It emphasizes the necessity of integrating flood mitigation strategies within urban planning to safeguard communities against flood hazards.
requested_output_constraints: * Introduction: A paragraph. An introduction to the field report along with any other sources. * Results: Two to three paragraphs. An explanation of the findings along with further implications. * Summary: A paragraph. A summary of the findings referring back to the intro.
- Be sure to only include relevant information. - Be sure to be in-depth with explanations.
Use only the supplied task context and input; do not retrieve or rely on outside sources.

prompt_text:
Task objective:
To assess whether there is a violation of the rules according to the Law on the Prevention of Domestic Violence for a given case.

Task procedure/context:
1) Review the details of the case to identify relevant facts and circumstances. 2) Compare these details against the legal criteria for domestic violence as defined in the applicable law.

Input specification:
* Case Details: As detailed as necessary. Information about the case, including the nature of the incident(s), identities of the involved parties, relationship between the parties, specific actions or behaviors alleged, and any evidence or testimony provided. * Legal Criteria for Domestic Violence: Describe how the court evaluates cases and determines appropriate measures to address domestic violence, such as restraining orders or counseling requirements. This may include types of behaviors that constitute domestic violence, the legal definitions involved, and any other relevant legal provisions or standards that need to be met for an act to be classified as domestic violence.

Supplied input:
**Input Sections**

**Case Details:**

A married couple, Ana (35) and Janez (38), have been experiencing marital issues for several months. Ana reports that Janez has increasingly subjected her to verbal abuse, including derogatory remarsk about her appearance and intelligence. Additionally, Janez has assumed control over their finances, closely monitoring Ana's spending and demanding accountability for every euro expended. 

During a recent alteraction, Janez hurled a glass at Ana, narrowly avoiding striking her head. Ana promptly notified the authorities, leading to the issuance of a temporary restrating order against Janez. She now seeks a permanent restraining order and contemplates initiating divorce proceedings. 

**Legal Criteria for Domestic Violence:**

The Slovenian Law on the Prevention of Domestic Violence defines domestic violence as any act of physical, psychological, or sexual violence committed against a family member. This includes spouses, partners, children, parents, and other relatives living in the same household. 

The law outlines various forms of abuse that constitute domestic violence, including:

* Physical violence: any intentional act of physical force that causes harm or injury to another person.
* Psychological violence: any intentional act that causes emotional distress or suffering, such as threats, insults, verbal abuse, or controlling behavior.
* Sexual violence: any non-consensual sexual act, including rape, sexual assault, and sexual harassment.

The court evaluates domestic violence cases based on evidence presented, including victim testimony, witness statements, police reports, and any medical records. If the court finds that domestic violence has occurred, it can issue a restraining order against the abuser, requiring them to stay away from the victim and refrain from further abuse. The court may also mandate counseling or other interventions for both parties.
requested_output_constraints: * Assessment: Analyze the case details in relation to the legal criteria for domestic violence. This involves assessing whether the actions or behaviors in the case meet the legal definitions and standards of domestic violence as set out in the law. * Conclusion on Legal Violation: Provide a conclusion based on the assessment, stating whether or not there is a violation of the Law on the Prevention of Domestic Violence in the given case. It should be backed by the analysis of how the case details align or do not align with the legal criteria.
The individuals involved in the proceedings must necessarily be members of the same family; otherwise, it does not qualify as domestic violence.
Use only the supplied task context and input; do not retrieve or rely on outside sources.

A summary of the document from an architecture & engineering perspective, including relevant drawings and reports. * Certification: 1 paragraph. Supplementary information, calculations or documentation to support the proposal.

Supplied input:
**Input Sections**

**Transcript:**

Please don’t call Alexander Payne’s ‘The Holdovers’ a return to form
For Payne, his homage to ’70s comedy-dramas is simply the next film

Perspective by Ann Hornaday
Chief film critic
October 27, 2023 at 6:00 a.m. EDT

Middleburg, Va. — Alexander Payne is speculating on how he’s gotten away with making the movies he wanted to make — literate, human comedy-dramas — for the past 27 years, during which literate, human comedy-dramas have become virtually extinct in Hollywood.

“I guess a lot of people — not a lot, but some — make such movies early in their careers and then are given the chance to do something quote-unquote big, and then never go back,” Payne says on a recent Saturday morning at the Middleburg Film Festival, where his new film “The Holdovers” was set to screen that night.

There’s a version of Payne’s career that could have gone very differently. His debut film, “Citizen Ruth,” came out in 1996, decades before young indie talents would be routinely hoovered up by the Comic Book Industrial Complex — a fate that, under different circumstances, might have been his.

“How do you know?” Payne asks sharply, adding that his creative and career decisions have always been based on one thing: the screenplay. “If I were in it for the money, I would have gone to law school like my parents wanted me to.”

Payne, 62, possesses the kind of courtesy, almost courtliness, associated with bygone notions of decorum and gentlemanly comportment. He’s unfailingly, almost self-consciously, polite. But that doesn’t mean he won’t push back over the course of a 45-minute interview that will pick up again during a post-screening Q&A. “How do you know?” “What does that mean?” “How so?” He peppers conversations with professorial challenges worthy of his protagonist in “The Holdovers,” a grumpy prep school teacher named Paul Hunham, portrayed with prickly bravura by Paul Giamatti.

“The Holdovers,” which opens in Washington on Nov. 3, takes place at the fictional Barton Academy over the Christmas holiday in 1970, when Hunham is tasked with looking after a group of students who aren’t able to join their families for the winter break. Ultimately, their number is reduced to one: a bright, disaffected junior named Angus Tully, played by newcomer Dominic Sessa. Together with the school’s cook, Mary Lamb (Da’Vine Joy Randolph), the lonely, motley crew form something of an ad hoc family, with all the bickering and bonding that one expects will ensue.

With its calibrated balance of humor and pathos, attunement to the details of human behavior and fine-grained realism, “The Holdovers” is of a piece with Payne’s past films, which include “Election,” “About Schmidt,” “The Descendants,” “Nebraska” and 2004’s “Sideways,” which also starred Giamatti. As Payne has said often while doing press for his latest film, it exemplifies the 1970s movies he has been trying to make throughout his career.

“Those films were imprinted on me, on us, the way musical taste is imprinted on us when we’re in our late teens, and it kind of doesn’t change for the rest of your life,” Payne explains, adding that he also loves the era as the last great golden age of American cinema, when an alchemy took place between the old and the new. “The commitment to literate, human comedies and dramas with good screenplays and good characters came out of studios and went onto the streets,” Payne continues, “and entered into a more modern vernacular where you can show nudity, say bad words, really approximate real life. But still within the context of well-structured, thoughtfully made, sensitive movies as interpreted by a new generation of artists.”

Well-structured, thoughtfully made and sensitive could apply as easily to “Election” and “The Descendants” as to “About Schmidt” and “Nebraska.” With “The Holdovers,” which was written by David Hemingson, Payne has taken his love for the sensibility one step further, into the visual and aural texture of the film itself. It opens with period-correct logos from Miramax and Focus Features, complete with pops and skips on the soundtrack; the rest of the movie has the wintry, slightly muted palette and lilting folk soundtrack that evoke Mike Nichols or Hal Ashby at their most wistfully humanistic.

“At some point, I just made the decision, ‘Huh, wouldn’t it be fun to make it look and sound as though it had been made in 1970?’” Payne recalled after the “Holdovers” screening at Middleburg. “I don’t remember at what point I thought that, but I thought it would be a fun little parlor trick to try.” But the last thing he wanted was kitsch. He cites “my aversion to a lot of period films that rub your nose in how period they are. ‘Look at this wallpaper, look at these cars, look at this hairdo, look at this wardrobe.’ Like, if they make the movie in 1958, everything is from 1958. It’s supposed to bring me into the movie and it takes me right out of the movie.” With “The Holdovers,” he says, “I wanted it to seem as grimy and banal as though we were making a low-budget film then, in 1970.”

Sessa, who plays a prep school student, and Giamatti, who plays one of the school's instructors, in another scene from “The Holdovers.” (Seacia Pavao/Focus Features/AP)
Payne knew he had succeeded when “The Holdovers” played the London Film Festival earlier this month; he sat next to the legendary editor and sound designer Walter Murch, who worked with Francis Ford Coppola on “The Conversation” and “Apocalypse Now,” and whom Payne called on for advice. After the screening, Murch commended Payne with a terse “Nice job.” Then, Payne recalls, “he said, ‘But you know what the most ’70s touch was?’ And I said, ‘No, what?’ He goes, ‘That they didn’t hug at the end. They shook hands.’ And I said, ‘I’ll see you and raise you: We didn’t even get a close-up of the hands clasping.’”

“The Holdovers” was filmed in New England (Sessa was a casting coup, having been recruited from the drama club at Deerfield Academy, one of several area schools that play Barton), continuing Payne’s dedication to filming on location, often using locals as supporting players. Although he owns a home in Topanga Canyon, he hasn’t made a movie in Los Angeles since he was a film student. “I have three arenas of life right now,” he explains. “I’m in Omaha for my 100-year-old mother. I’m in Athens, Greece, for my 6-year-old daughter. Then, with whatever time is left, I have some filmmaking to try to do. I’ve got career, mother, daughter.” (Payne has been married and divorced twice, from the actress Sandra Oh and from Maria Kontos, who lives in Greece with their daughter.)

Payne grew up in Omaha, where his father ran a 24-hour restaurant (Payne’s mother was a professor of French and Spanish at a local college). When he graduated from Stanford in 1983 (he missed his 40th reunion to attend Middleburg), he applied to five film schools and Columbia journalism school — the latter of which aligns not only with his dedication to documentarylike authenticity, but also with the curiosity that has animated all of his movies. “It’s all the human story,” he says, noting that, had he become a journalist, “my dream job would have been, like, Buenos Aires bureau chief of The Post or the Times or the Miami Herald or something like that. … A career like [New York Times reporter] Alan Riding’s: Madrid, Buenos Aires, Rio, Paris. What a groovy career he had.”

Instead, Payne went to film school at UCLA, where, he recalls, “they encouraged the art spirit and, for lack of a less pretentious term, the auteur spirit. We were proud of Coppola having attended there, [and] Alex Cox, Charles Burnett, the Doors — the Doors met there.” After breaking out with “Citizen Ruth,” a stinging social satire about abortion politics starring Laura Dern, Payne enjoyed a strong run of films that met with critical and, particularly in the case of “Sideways” and “The Descendants,” commercial success. (Payne won Oscars for the screenplays he co-wrote for both films.)

In 2017, Payne directed the futuristic satire “Downsizing” from a script he co-wrote with his frequent collaborator, Jim Taylor. As a sci-fi fantasy — about a world in which people need to shrink to take advantage of dwindling resources — it was a major departure for Payne. It not only bombed at the box office, but also was the worst-reviewed film of what until then had been a preternaturally charmed career. Payne’s memories of the project are mixed. “It was a bit arduous to make,” he says today. “I didn’t enjoy doing visual effects. That stuff’s for the birds. It’s hard enough to shoot people in a car, or people sitting around a table. And then add endless hours of ‘Hmm, there’s not enough contrast in the cloud.’ Who cares?”

He watched “Downsizing” again this past summer, at an environmentally themed film festival in Greece. “I’m still proud of many passages in it, and of midwifing Hong Chau’s performance,” he says. “There’s a very good passage about a half-hour, 40 minutes into the film, where you follow Matt Damon being downsized, that was very impressive to me. And the music is very good … In about 800 years, when everyone actually is small, it will be hailed as a masterpiece.”

Payne says of his latest film, “I wanted it to seem as grimy and banal as though we were making a low-budget film then, in 1970.” (Amanda Andrade-Rhoades for The Washington Post)
Payne had been wanting to do a film like “The Holdovers” for years when, out of the blue, Hemingson sent him a script for a television pilot set at a boarding school; Payne told Hemingson he didn’t want to direct the pilot but asked him to create a script for a feature project that takes place in the same world. Although “The Holdovers” reunites him with Giamatti and shares tonal DNA with his past work, Payne considers it simply his latest movie. “I’m getting questions like, ‘Is this a return to form?’ or ‘Is this a reaction to “Downsizing”?’ You know, ‘going back to a nice, small, human film’? And I say, ‘No, it’s just what the next film is.’ And if it’s more in the pattern of what my films previous to ‘Downsizing’ were, well, it’s just who I am.”

Albert Berger, who with his partner Ron Yerxa produced “Election” and “Nebraska,” had seen an earlier cut of “The Holdovers” but saw the final version at Middleburg. What he saw was “a director, completely on top of his game, who’s able to convey the depth of the human experience, all within an image of two sisters sitting on a bed, or an outdoor bookstore in the snow, or in the way an extra delivers a line. His films are alive with comedy, pain and grace.”

Those were the values that drew Seiji McCarthy, a bespoke shoemaker in Tokyo, to Payne’s films, especially “The Descendants,” which McCarthy re-watched last spring and then emailed Payne (they’re both Stanford graduates). Payne wound up inviting McCarthy to Middleburg, where he sat cross-legged on the couch in McCarthy’s hotel room and asked him about his life for an hour and a half; then McCarthy measured Payne for a pair of shoes.

For McCarthy, the experience was akin to watching one of Payne’s movies. “I found talking to him, and the entire experience at Middleburg, very human, in the best sense of the word,” McCarthy wrote later in an email. “He seems genuinely interested in the human experience — not just his own, but in general and across gender, age, culture, etc. — which is reflected in both his art and in the conversations he has with people.”

Payne agrees with some observers that his films have softened recently, especially since “Sideways.” There are moments of lacerating humor in “The Holdovers,” especially when Hunham is insulting his most lackadaisical students. But there are moments of aching, unapologetic tenderness as well. “With aging, you value emotion more,” Payne observes simply. “And you don’t have that knee-jerk adolescent-based or American-based suspicion of emotion.”

That’s about as far as Payne will go in explaining what “The Holdovers,” or any of his movies, mean. Fans might see a clear through-line, whether the films have to do with road trips, father-son relationships or the turning of a curmudgeonly heart — all of which are on full display in “The Holdovers.” For Payne, however, questions of theme are best left unanswered.

“It’s not my job to talk about theme,” Payne says. “I might get it wrong, too. When I’m making a movie, I’m the one who most knows what it should be. When I’m done making a movie, I’m the one who least knows what that movie is. … I’ll need about 10 years or 15 years to go by and not see it, and then watch it and go, ‘Oh, now I see what they were talking about.’”

The statement is written using pre-prepared DNA results and statistical analyses which are converted from electronic reports on our laboratory information management system to a written report the court can digest.

We also access the raw DNA profile, and the interpreted DNA profile for the exhibits but also for and person samples which are used to compare to the exhibits. Finally we access the results of statistical interpretation software which analyses the exhibits and compares person samples to them to generate a statistical assessment for the likelihood a person contributed DNA to that mixture. We collate all of this information which is located in our laboratory information management system into a written document which is easy for the courts to read and understand.

Supplied input:
**Input Sections**

**Sample Details:**
1.  Case and Forensic Scientist Details:
    -   Case Title: State of California v. John Doe
    -   Case Number: 2023-CR-001234
    -   Date of Report: February 15, 2024
    -   Forensic Scientist: Dr. Jane Smith, Ph.D., Forensic Scientist, Accredited by the American Academy of Forensic Sciences (AAFS)
2.  Exhibits Received:
    -   Batch 1:
        -   Received Date: January 10, 2024
        -   Location: Los Angeles Police Department, Central Division
        -   Exhibit Descriptions:
            -   Exhibit 1: Bloodstained knife

    -   Exhibit 1 - Bloodstained Knife:
        -   Physical Description: Serrated kitchen knife, 6-inch blade, stained with blood, damage to the tip and bent blade
        -   DNA Analysis: Full DNA profile obtained, matching the victim's profile from Exhibit 2
        -   Statistical Analysis: STRmix software, likelihood of random individual other than victim contributing DNA is 1 in 1 billion
    -   Exhibit 2 - Cotton Swab with Suspected Blood:
        -   DNA Analysis: Full DNA profile obtained from swab, matching the victim's DNA

**Summary:**

The United States has a long and complex history of border control policy. Beginning with the Reagan Era, border enforcement began to increase significantly, with a focus on preventing the entry of undocumented immigrants from Mexico. This trend continued under subsequent administrations, with each president implementing new policies and initiatives aimed at further securing the border. 

In the subsequent decades, President Clinton first signed the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, which increased penalties for illegal immigration and made it more difficult for undocumented immigrants to obtain legal status. In the aftermath of the 9/11 attacks, border security became even more of a priority, with the creation of the Department of Homeland Security and the implementation of new security measures. And under President Obama and Trump, ICE detention centers became center piece which showed significant human rights abuses.

**Shift to Industrialism:**

The U.S. border control policy has undergone a dramatic shift towards industrialism in the last half century. This is evident in the increasing militarization of the border, with the construction of fences, walls, and other barriers, as well as the deployment of thousands of Border Patrol agents. The use of technology has also increased significantly, with the implementation of drones, sensors, and other surveillance equipment. This shift has been driven by several factors, including the perceived threat of terrorism, the rise of drug trafficking, and the growing number of undocumented immigrants.

One of the most significant events that shaped U.S. border policy was the 9/11 terrorist attacks. In response to the attacks, the U.S. government implemented a series of measures to enhance domestic security, including increased border security. This led to a significant increase in funding for the Department of Homeland Security, which is responsible for border control. As a result of these measures, the number of Border Patrol agents stationed on the U.S.-Mexico border has more than doubled since 2001. 

Additionally, the amount of money spent on border security has increased dramatically, from $4.2 billion in 2001 to over $13 billion in 2016. Because 2010s has seen an even bigger technological developments in the militarization and gun manufacturing companies, which pivoted their interests into border policy.

**Decade of interest:**

We will be analyzing border control policies during the 2000s.

**Title:** The Influence of Meteorological Variables on CO2 Emissions

**Abstract:**
This study investigates the impact of meteorological variables on CO2 emissions using random forest analysis. The results indicate that meteorological variables significantly impact CO2 emissions, explaining a substantial portion of the variance in PM2.5 concentrations.

**Introduction:**

This study examines the relationship between meteorological variables and CO2 emissions, contributing to our understanding of the factors influencing air pollution.

Higher temperatures and humidity contribute to increased PM2.5 concentrations, likely due to enhanced chemical reactions and reduced dispersion. Conversely, stronger winds promote air circulation and reduce pollutant accumulation.

Task procedure/context:
The procedure for writing a research proposal in governmental environmental action starts with the analysis of scientific accumulated data, with the latest information provided taken as basis, preferably from IPCC or UNFCCC. The proposal should outline the weaknesses or flaws in the current system under the control of governments, in an attempt to ensure possible solutions with clarity, maintainability and verifiability.

Input specification:
* Overview: (2-3 paragraphs) General overview of the state of climate change and governmental actions so far in conjunction with intergovernmental deals such as Paris Agreement.  * Current Flaws: (5-7 paragraphs) The summary of current systems in place that are colliding with governmental/intergovernmental climate action.  * Missing Legal Governmental Policies: (4-6 paragraphs) Overview of the various areas where developed nations and governments lack in climate policy in relation to deregulation.

Supplied input:
**Input Sections**

# Research Proposal: Sustainability Transition at the Governmental Level

**Overview:**

Climate change is one of the most pressing issues facing humanity today. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has warned that global warming is likely to reach 1.5°C between 2030 and 2052 if greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise at the current rate. This will have devastating consequences for the planet, including more extreme weather events, rising sea levels, and mass extinctions.

Governments around the world have taken some action to address climate change, most notably by signing the Paris Agreement in 2015. However, the agreement is non-binding, and many governments are not doing enough to meet their emissions reduction targets. As a result, there is a growing consensus that more needs to be done to achieve a sustainable transition to a low-carbon economy.

**Current Flaws:**

One of the biggest flaws in the current system is the short-termism of governments and corporations. Politicians are often focused on winning the next election, and corporations are focused on maximizing profits for shareholders. This leads to a focus on short-term economic growth at the expense of long-term environmental sustainability.

On that basis, regulation and monitoring of the corporations is a huge problem as these interest groups usually work to convince politicians by making huge donations to their campaigns, which leads to politicians making decisions that favor them, despite the accumulated data, activism participation, and organization.

Another flaw is the influence of the fossil fuel industry. Fossil fuel companies have a vested interest in maintaining the status quo, and they have used their power and wealth to lobby governments and influence public opinion. This has made it difficult to enact policies that would reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

Also, most of the initiatives that are taken usually have loopholes in them. For example, many corporations usually create their operations in other regions or even countries such as Bangladesh, Indonesia, etc., creating a much cheaper workforce, while not being subject to climate-change-related quotas that they would be subject to in their own countries such as the U.S. or Canada.

Finally, there is a lack of public awareness and understanding of climate change. Many people are not aware of the seriousness of the problem, and they are not sure what they can do to help. This makes it difficult to build public support for ambitious climate action.

**Missing Legal Governmental Policies:**

Despite the urgent need for action, many developed nations still lack the necessary legislation to address climate change effectively. Input specification:
* Communication Requirements: 1 paragraphs, 2-3 sentences. User should define the communication needs and the technical demands such as bit rate, latency, distance between receiver and transmitter and more. * Transmission medium: 1 paragraphs, 4-5 sentences. User should specify under what medium the signal has to pass through, given that - the AI can chose between different optical based recommendation, for example - an led with a higher beam divergence would be more beneficial under water in comparison to lasers. In space, lasers are a game changer and using the unique specifications of lasers we are able to achieve a lot of great stuff.

Supplied input:
**Input Sections**

**Communication Requirements:**
The optical communication system should be capable of transmitting data at a rate of 1 Gbps over a distance of 500 km in space. The latency should be minimized, with a target of less than 10 milliseconds. The system should be reliable and capable of operating under varying environmental conditions.

When considering the "Error Rate" - the system must maintain a low bit error rate (BER) not exceeding 1 in 10^12 bits, to guarantee the accuracy of transmitted data.

Some of the optical communication system operates directly from space and therefor are stationed there, these systems must exhibit robustness against varying environmental conditions, including temperature fluctuations, cosmic radiation, solar interference and also colliding with other celestial bodies. In space - the systems should operate flawlessly within a temperature range of -20C degrees to 50C degrees, ensuring reliable performance under extreme conditions.
Another issue in systems stationed in space is the availability in space, the system should demonstrate high power efficiency, therefor the power consumption during data transmission should not exceed 5 watts per Gbps, enabling sustainable operation over extended mission durations.

**Transmission Medium:**
The transmission medium is space itself, presenting unique challenges and opportunities for optical communication. In the vacuum of space, the system exploits the advantages of utilizing one of the characteristics of lasers, which is the ability to produce a very narrow beamwidth, prompting high data rates and efficient transmission. The laser beam divergence is carefully controlled, aiming for an angular spread of less than 1 milliradians in order to ensure optimal signal concentration.
This adjustment accurately reflects that it is the absence of atmospheric turbulence, not the lack of atmosphere itself, that enables the use of lasers with narrow beamwidths in space.

Although space acts as transmission medium can present good opportunities, it also presents very unique challenges. Celestial objects in space pose potential obstacles and risks to the transmission path. For instance, one of the major problems in transmitting to long distances is the risk that the light beam will diverge greatly while moving near massive objects, this effect call "gravitational lensing", and in order to address this issue a precise trajectory planning and adaptive optics systems are integrated. Using these systems enable real time adjustments to the laser's beam focus, minimizing the impact of gravitational lensing and optimizing the link quality.

Supplied input:
**Input Sections**

**Manuscript for publication:**

**Rethinking the Role of Intuition in Moral Judgment**

**Introduction**

Intuition has long been considered a central feature of moral judgment. It is often described as a quick, automatic, and non-inferential process that provides us with immediate access to moral truths. However, recent empirical research has challenged this traditional view, suggesting that intuition may not be as reliable or fundamental as once thought.

**The Traditional View of Intuition**

According to the traditional view, moral intuitions are innate and self-evident. They are believed to be based on a special faculty that allows us to apprehend moral principles directly. This view has been defended by philosophers such as Immanuel Kant, who argued that we have a "moral sense" that enables us to recognize the rightness or wrongness of actions.

**Empirical Challenges**

In recent years, a growing body of empirical research has cast doubt on the traditional view of intuition. Studies have shown that moral intuitions can be influenced by a variety of factors, including culture, emotion, and cognitive biases. For example, research has found that people from different cultures often have different moral intuitions about issues such as abortion and euthanasia.

**The Role of Emotion**

One important factor that has been found to influence moral intuitions is emotion. Studies have shown that when people are feeling certain emotions, such as disgust or anger, they are more likely to make negative moral judgments. This suggests that moral intuitions may not be purely cognitive processes, but may also involve an emotional component.

**Cognitive Biases**

Another factor that can influence moral intuitions is cognitive biases. These are systematic errors in thinking that can lead us to make incorrect judgments. For example, the framing effect occurs when the way in which information is presented influences our decisions, even if the underlying facts are the same. Studies have shown that the framing effect can also influence moral intuitions.

**A New Model of Moral Judgment**

Based on the empirical evidence, it is clear that the traditional view of intuition is inadequate. Instead, we need a new model of moral judgment that takes into account the influence of emotion and cognitive biases. One such model is the social intuitionist model, which proposes that moral judgments are primarily driven by social and emotional factors, rather than by abstract reasoning.

**Conclusion**

The role of intuition in moral judgment is complex and multifaceted. While intuition may still play a role in some aspects of moral decision-making, it is no longer seen as a reliable or fundamental guide. Instead, moral judgments are best understood as the product of a complex interplay of social, emotional, and cognitive factors.

    * Author, A. A. (Year). Title of article. *Journal Name*, volume(issue), page numbers.

**Transcript:**

Tiffany Young Talks Touring, Songwriting On Her Own Terms: ‘I Feel Like I Can Bare My Soul’

Tiffany Young talks about her 'Lips on Lips' project and more in this exclusive interview.

By Tamar Herman 

As a member of Girls’ Generation, Tiffany Young spent much of her life as part of the inner circles of K-pop royalty. The 29-year-old spent much of her teens and twenties living a life so different from that of the average person, she may as well have been living in a fantasy.

But after leaving Girls’ Generation’s label SM Entertainment at the end of 2017 the California-born Young reoriented her direction and started to release solo music aimed at English-speaking audiences. This year saw her release the fairy tale-inspired Lips on Lips and hold her first showcase tour throughout North America, during which she got up close and personal with her fans, both old and new, in a variety of intimate venues.

Ahead of her New York City show at the Bowery Ballroom on March 6, Young sat down with Billboard to talk about writing Lips on Lips, her inspirations and a whole lot more.

How’s the tour going?

Amazing. My favorite part about creating music is going on tour, and I haven’t been on tour in a while. I’m happy, nervous and excited all at the same time. This is the closest I’ve been to [the fans] so it’s really special.

What’s that been like for you?

It’s so rare you get a second chance. And the fact that I get to live those first time moments again, it’s special.

How is it different from your last first times?

It’s more intimate and personal because it’s the music I wrote. I feel like I can bare my soul. I feel so loved and accepted and ready to take on that energy to write and be more open. Because, in the end, opening up has always been the battle for me. I’m so glad I get to talk about this with you. It’s such an exciting time. Being on stage, I become the woman I want to be. It was such a magical feeling the other night [opening night in Toronto on March 3]. I’m rarely happy after a first show. I got off that stage and was like, “Dang, all that practice. All those rehearsals, all those nights and nights and days and days of just singing my heart out, or going to vocal lessons.” Everyone was like, “Why are you going to vocal lessons?” And I was just like, “Don’t ask.” I’m just going to always stay humble to my craft. It’s magical.

How has your singing style changed since you started taking vocal lessons?

It’s opened me up so much. It’s gotten me much more technical, but it’s gotten me back to the raw emotions as well. I’m not looking at real sheet music anymore, I’m just singing to my emotions. If I want to crescendo, I’ll crescendo to my heart beat, not a rule. It feels amazing.

How does it feel to be moving forward, past the first part of your career?

I was ready to go forward and do it. I’m ready to build, I’m ready to earn that time and love that [the fans] spend on me. Their hard-earned money, and the time they dedicate. I wanted to be worth a hundred, million times more. I wanted to be priceless. That when they come, it’s not even about that. It’s about getting in tune with their emotions, opening up and just getting to enjoy music the way it touched me too.

You just released Lips on Lips, and the tour is based on it. Why did you base everything around the title song, “Lips on Lips”?

My lifelong inspiration has been based on fairy-tale fantasies. I never hid from that, and I realized it’s because I believe that no matter the struggle or the obstacle or that fight that you’re going through, there’s always a happily ever after, there’s always a moment of triumph or that fairy-tale kiss, which was that moment in the EP. I laid it out like a book, where it’s a different chapter. You go from “Born Again” to searching for love to finding and romanticizing love, which was “Lips on Lips.” “Lips on Lips” was that moment where I was back in my happy space; I loved music because it made me feel better. And no matter how sad I was, it always came back to a happy song or a song about love, or a song about fighting through it with a smile. And “Lips on Lips” is where I got back to the hopeless romantic in me. I wanted to write a happy love song. Like, “Can I have fun now? I think I’m ready to have some fun now!” I really wanted to make it into a body of work, where there’s a story for each [song], backing each other up. I wanted it to be something that’s memorable. I wanted it to be very true to me. I’m very glad. It’s not far from what I’ve always been talking about: fairy tale fantasy.

What’s your favorite fairy tale?

The Little Mermaid. I realized that the psychology of why I loved it so much was because she was in her world where everybody was telling her that she had everything, and she was a princess. But she believed that she could break out of that and find love in a bigger world. And I guess that’s what I kind of have always been searching for, and I’m happy to be back in a bigger world.

Do you have a favorite fictional kiss?

My favorite kiss scene…Titanic. As heartbreaking as the ending is, those [scenes] are my favorites. Romeo & Juliet is always a favorite. Anything Baz Luhrmann, who everyone knows I’m a huge fan of. And La La Land. Recently, I was watching Never Been Kissed just to go back to it. I think all my references have kind of seeped into me deep enough, so I got to write Lips on Lips. I got back to where I want to feel fluffy and romantic.

Rom-com-y?

Yea! And my new favorite would be Crazy Rich Asians. That last scene on the plane. Everybody needs fairy tales, everybody needs that hopeless romantic rekindled back in them.

How has your approach to music changed since you first began releasing songs under the name Tiffany Young last year?

I am K-pop. I am Korean. I want to keep that in me. And I want to bring that to the table, and learn from the masters of pop, which I am still kind of mind-boggled over. Of the amazing producers and writers that I got to work with. Obviously, Kevin [Nish of Far East Movement, who also manages Young under the group’s Transparent Agency]. Still only the Asian-American act to have a [Hot 100] No. 1 record. I remember asking Kevin about continuing music. I was like, “Why do you think I should continue?” He was like, “Because I believe in change.” I was sold. I’m so lucky to have a team and a leader who gave me that answer versus, “Because it’s your life.” It’s not about us. It’s about everybody else and about the world, and the future for everybody else. Which led to Fernando Garibay, and Kris [Khristopher Riddick-Tynes] from The Rascals. John Yip from The Stereotypes is a very big part of this project. So I have all my brothers who are like, “We want you to win. We want change. We want to see an Asian-American. We want to see an Asian woman.”

Being around the masters and experts, those producers have definitely let me learn and open up and create the best of what I love in both worlds. So I think that, if ever, I’ve been loving everything about Korean music more. I’ve been loving everything about American music more. I just want to keep writing. Because it’s tough, getting into your emotions and finding the right things to say. But I must say, it’s getting much more detailed and expressive.

Have you faced any difficulties as you hone this new songwriting skill of yours?

There are times when I’m like, “Am I cut out for writing?” I ask myself that every couple of songs, when I get stuck. Like “The Flower,” for instance. I wrote it over and over. I had some amazing collaborators in the room. I had 9AM, who are new producers signed to The Stereotypes. I had Satica, my musical goddess, and Varren Wade, who did Ella Mai’s “Trip.” So we had such a cool mix of collaborators in the room. And we wrote it, then I rewrote it so many times until it became what it is now. I realized that once you find something and you keep pulling it apart, you stop being afraid. And I want to stop being afraid. That’s why I got to do 12 years of what I’ve done, and now I’m ready. And I hope it inspires future girl bands and female soloists and women in music. I just think about that girl who was lost at 11, and think about how [music] touched me and saved me, and how I could possibly do that for somebody else. That’s the magical feeling, that’s the only reason why I’m here. It’s been great to go back to my roots and my inner deepest, darkest crevices. And, you know, it made “The Flower,” going there.

How was it working with Kenny “Babyface” Edmonds on “Runaway”?

I really, really wanted to work with The Rascals. I started working with Kris and Antonio Dixon, who are part of the Babyface camp, and I went to the studio almost every day for a good three months. I felt like I was going to SM again. It was kind of that system. I would see Kenny every other day or so and be like, well, not “annyeonghaseyo” but like, “Hey, I go here. I practice and write everyday!” And it just became so organic. We were looking for a sound and a story that really honed into the fairytale lane. I realized the moment there was the opportunity to write and collaborate with Babyface — I did my research. I wanted to know what type of instrument I wanted to start the song with. I wanted that classic fairy tale love song that Babyface is such a master of creating. It’s such a dream come true. It was an amazing opportunity to go into the studio. Take the time, get to know me more, and get to learn from legends. It’s still such an amazing moment, and I’m so blessed.
Do you feel that the songs are all different stories about you? Are they connected together so that Lips on Lips tells one story about Tiffany Young?

It wasn’t a specific story, but more everything that is there about me. I believed in love, which goes back to the Little Mermaid story, and I ran away to Korea. I’m running away once again. Not running away. I had a great time, and they let me — my bandmates were like, “You spoke it into existence.” It was also so, so rewarding when I let my bandmates hear “Runaway.” A majority of them cried. Like, “This is the song I always imagined you doing.” And I was just like, “Stop crying!” It felt amazing. But that’s when I know it’s real, because they know me inside out so they’d let me know if it’s good or not.

The song that resonates with a lot of listeners is the introspective “Not Barbie.” Why is the song’s message something you wanted to focus on?

Growing up, I didn’t see enough representation through media. I think now is the perfect time, because there’s so much diversity going on, and it’s beautiful. Now more than ever, we’re talking about strength and vulnerability, and finding the differences in us to be the most beautiful parts about us. I wanted to open up about a physical condition that I had my whole life — severe scoliosis — and how that takes a toll mentally, physically, and emotionally. I wanted to open up so that anyone who feels the same way, who feels like they’re limited or that a certain situation or condition is pulling them back. I hope it inspires them to go further and push themselves further into being the best they can be. And making that the best part of them. I’ve said it multiple times. Being positively true to yourself, body and soul, is the most beautiful thing. There’s nothing else. I wanted to be able to say that very, very boldly because of the K-pop background. Because of the Asian background. I think it’s a story that relates to everyone. Any woman or man, or girl or boy, of color, of shape or form or condition, you name it. I always wanted to write something that would be uplifting.

Do you feel that “Not Barbie” goes hand in hand with last year’s “Over My Skin”?

It definitely does. I say it during the show too, but damn, it feels so good to be a woman. Because it’s not about pleasing others but about how you want to feel, and you being amazing without needing or wanting validation from anybody else. And that comes from finding self-acceptance. And when that self-acceptance comes in, you celebrate those imperfections and you make them your strength. “Over My Skin” happened fast because I was like, “I’m home! I wanna do this.” But I actually wrote “Not Barbie” during that same time. We just came out with the bolder, more fun message first.

You actually are very Barbie blonde right now. Was it a nod to the song?

For me, what I love about K-pop is that it’s 50% auditory [experience], and 50% visual. I love creating concepts and things around it. I wanted to do something new. I’ve never gone this platinum blonde before, and I think it’s a statement when you’re really sacrificing every strand of hair on your head for your creation. It’s definitely bringing something different out in me too. I guess it’s my new superhero suit. I hope it lets everybody be bold and try different hair colors.

How do you feel about your relationship with womanhood?

I’m thankful for all the incredible women in my life. From my mom then to my aunt to my sister, and then to my [Girls’ Generation] sisters. That it’s about celebrating each other, and it’s about beauty in every age. And that your imperfections, your scars are what make you strong and beautiful. I loved growing up. I loved being able to wear certain things, be a certain way. I think I really, really embraced that growing up with a group of girlfriends as well. I told them, “We get to wear this now! We get to try this now!” I think it’s still not talked about enough in Asian culture or Asian-American representation, that women are beautiful in every age. And hopefully me continuously doing what I do can show that. It’s not about what’s on the outside, but it’s that strength and that heart to continue. Showing that resilience and strength is what I hope shines.

An archetype is a universal, recurring pattern or symbol that represents a fundamental aspect of human nature or experience. In literature, archetypes are often used to represent certain types of characters, such as the hero, the villain, the mentor, and the trickster.

Some common archetypes in literature include:
* The Hero: A protagonist who embodies courage, strength, and determination.
* The Mentor: A wise and experienced figure who guides the hero.
* The Shadow: A character who represents the dark side of the hero or the forces that oppose them.
* The Trickster: A character who uses cunning and deception to achieve their goals.

Task objective:
Writing an agenda that meets legal requirements for a council meeting 

Task procedure/context:
An agenda sets the framework for a council meeting and provides enough information for the public to be aware of the matters that will be discussed, whether a conclusion is being sought as part of the discussion, and whether there are any associated deadlines. The agenda must meet legal requirements to hold a meeting that has given due notice to allow the public to either attend or submit comments and concerns, that it meets legal requirements for meeting logistics, that it is quorate to ensure democracy is upheld, and that any decisions being considered are not reached illegally.

Input specification:
* Format: The format of the agenda must be in line with government guidance, meeting legal requirements, and be clear and concise and with the correct information such as headers/titles, the nature of the business, any deadlines that need to be considered etc.  * Content: The content must be worded to allow the public to understand what will be discussed, and posed as a question that the council will be considering, and if possible, the outcome that will be sought. For example: To discuss whether to fund a new sports centre at the local park. Lay language sound be used and any technical terms explained.  * Attachments: Any appendices must be clear and concise and any question/item proposed needs to have sufficient information in order for a decision to be reached. of example: The above discussion about a sports centre should set out the costs, any public consultations and identifying needs, and the proposed method of funding. Where confidential papers are required this needs to be clearly marked and sent to only those who require them, but also noted on the cover sheet so the public are aware the information is confidential. However, this should only be used when absolutely necessary and in line with legal advice that suggests why something should be confidential. 

Supplied input:
**Input Sections**

**Format:**

* Header: Local Council Meeting Agenda
* Title: Regular Meeting of the [Council Name]
* Date and Time: [Date] at [Time]
* Location: [Meeting Location]

**Content:**

* Call to Order: To establish quorum and commence the meeting.
* Apologies of absence.
* Declaration of Interests.
* Approval of Minutes: To review and approve the minutes from the previous meeting dated X.
* Public Comments: To provide an opportunity for members of the public to address the council on matters within its jurisdiction. The Council does not have to provide a verbal response and may respond in writing at a later date, the response of which will be made public.
* Discussion Item: To discuss, and make any applicable recommendations, as whether to fund a new sports centre at the local park (appendix x)
* Action Item: To consider a proposal to approve the construction of a new library and to make any applicable recommendations (appendix x)
* Press and public asked to leave the meeting as per Standing Orders and LGA (1972) due to the confidential nature of the following item*
* Closed Session: To discuss pending litigation as permitted under Government Code Section 54956.9.
* Press and public to be readmitted to the meeting. 
* Adjournment of meeting.

**Attachments:**

* Appendix A: Cost estimates and public consultation results for the proposed sports centre.
* Appendix B: Architectural plans and budget for the proposed library.
* Appendix C: Confidential legal memorandum regarding pending litigation (distributed only to council members).
requested_output_constraints: * Cover sheet: This acts as the public notice and must include the title of the meeting, the location, date and time of the meeting, as well as the nature of the business to be discussed. It should include any information relating to legal bindings such as filming or recording the meeting and whether there is the ability to submit written representation as well as any deadlines that should be adhered to. * Agenda itself: Must be in clear English in a way a lay person can understand, formatted to 'in house' standards and government guidance, and produced in a standard font type and size as well as variabilities for disabled persons should this be required. * Associated papers: Clearly marked to correspond to agenda items, with correct titles and formatting and full information that meeds legal requirements, with confidential papers sent separately.

On first glance agendas seem simple but there is significant understanding that must go into the preparation to make sure that not only are legal requirements met but that also the papers are clear enough to encourage public engagement. Preciseness is key for clear language and short sentences. Best practices are: to prepare drafts in advance and run them by the chairman, as well as have a fresh pair of eyes look over the finished compilation to spot any errors. Common mistakes:1)  include information only items that have no need to be on the agenda to inflate the perception of the importance of the meetings and/or extend the meeting time. Only items that require a decision should be included. 2) not correctly counting clear days' notice and getting confused about bank holidays and/or weekends.

Task objective:
Write a method for network analysis of microbial communities.

Task procedure/context:
Microbial network analysis is a popular technique to explore large microbial datasets. In these networks, nodes represent taxa and edges represent direct or indirect associations between taxa. A method should be provided that is capable of performing network analysis of microbial datasets. It should ensure scalability.

Input specification:
* Method aim: A paragraph about the goal of the network analysis and essential details like what parameters are used for network construction.

Supplied input:
**Input Sections**

**Method aim:**

The aim of this network analysis is to investigate the co-occurrence and co-exclusion relationships between microbial taxa within 16S rRNA gene sequencing data. This will be achieved by constructing a microbial association network, where nodes represent taxa and edges represent statistically significant co-occurrence or co-exclusion relationships. The network will be constructed based on the SparCC correlation coefficient. Additionally, the edge weights will be based on the absolute value of the SparCC coefficient, reflecting the strength of the association between taxa. Scalability is paramount in microbial network analysis due to the sheer complexity and volume of data involved. SparCC focuses on identifying sparse correlations, meaning it only calculates correlations between taxa that exhibit significant associations. This sparsity reduces computational complexity, making SparCC suitable for large datasets. A correlation threshold of 0.6 and p-value of 0.05 will be used in this protocol.

Logical Argumentation Analysis - evaluating the logical structure of arguments

Task procedure/context:
In philosophy, it is imperative that we identify fallacies or inconsistencies in someone's reasoning, as such "jumps" make arguments invalid. Thus, we always have to check if an argument "makes sense".

Input specification:
* Textual data: The philosophical texts/arguments themselves. * Logical argument Structure: 2 paragraphs. Information about how the foundations of the arguments are related to each other and how they lead to the conclusions. * Logical operators: 1 paragraph. **Input Sections**

**Textual Data:**

"Mohists rail against the most fundamental assumptions of Confucianism, namely the priority of filial piety as a source for cultivating positive moral psychology and the importance of rites and rituals in cultivating virtues capable of guiding action in accordance with yi (Mozi). They see the privileged and special bonds of family as problematically impeding establishment of jian ai, the excess of rituals as unnecessarily wasteful, and the perspectivism of Daoism as unacceptably anarchic and morally relativistic (Chan, 1963). For the Mohist, society requires unity of purpose and values as the foundation for calculating and justly distributing benefit (Johnston, 2013). This is clear evidence of strong criticality of tradition."

**Logical Argument Structure:**

Paragraph 1:
- Mohists criticize the Confucian assumptions of filial piety and rituals as the basis for moral development.
- They argue that these assumptions hinder the establishment of universal love (jian ai).
- Mohists view family bonds as an obstacle to jian ai.
- They consider excessive rituals to be wasteful.
- They reject the perspectivism of Daoism as leading to moral relativism.

**Logical Operators:**

- "namely" - indicates a specific example
- "and" - connects multiple criticisms of Confucianism
- "as" - introduces a reason for the criticisms

**Context Information:**

- Mohists and Confucians are two ancient Chinese philosophical schools.
- Jian ai refers to the concept of universal love or equal concern for all.
- Yi is a Confucian virtue that refers to righteousness or right action.

Input specification:
* Previous Measurements: Historical data, including measurements of various parameters like temperature, pH, pollutant levels, and other relevant water quality indicators. These measurements serve as a baseline to track changes over time. * Acceptable Ranges: Guidelines or standards that define the acceptable ranges for each parameter. These ranges indicate the water quality criteria that the river should meet for various uses, such as drinking water supply, recreation, or ecological health. * Warning Limitations: Specific limits or thresholds that trigger warnings or actions when a parameter exceeds them, indicating potential issues or pollution events. These limitations help in the early detection and response to water quality problems. * Updated Records: Incorporating recent observations and measurements of parameters, such as temperature, pH, and pollutant levels, into the historical data records.

    - The average pH during the same period was 7.4, ranging from 7.0 to 7.9.

prompt_text:
Task objective:
Writing an agenda that meets legal requirements for a council meeting 

Task procedure/context:
An agenda sets the framework for a council meeting and provides enough information for the public to be aware of the matters that will be discussed, whether a conclusion is being sought as part of the discussion, and whether there are any associated deadlines. The agenda must meet legal requirements to hold a meeting that has given due notice to allow the public to either attend or submit comments and concerns, that it meets legal requirements for meeting logistics, that it is quorate to ensure democracy is upheld, and that any decisions being considered are not reached illegally.

Input specification:
* Format: The format of the agenda must be in line with government guidance, meeting legal requirements, and be clear and concise and with the correct information such as headers/titles, the nature of the business, any deadlines that need to be considered etc.  * Content: The content must be worded to allow the public to understand what will be discussed, and posed as a question that the council will be considering, and if possible, the outcome that will be sought. For example: To discuss whether to fund a new sports centre at the local park. Lay language sound be used and any technical terms explained.  * Attachments: Any appendices must be clear and concise and any question/item proposed needs to have sufficient information in order for a decision to be reached. of example: The above discussion about a sports centre should set out the costs, any public consultations and identifying needs, and the proposed method of funding. Where confidential papers are required this needs to be clearly marked and sent to only those who require them, but also noted on the cover sheet so the public are aware the information is confidential. However, this should only be used when absolutely necessary and in line with legal advice that suggests why something should be confidential. 

Supplied input:
**Input Sections**

**Format:** The agenda for the City Council Meeting is structured to follow formal protocols, ensuring clear navigation through sections like "Welcome and Introductions," "Approval of Minutes," and "Public Comments." Each agenda item is clearly labeled, facilitating easy reference during the meeting.

**Content:**
1.  Welcome and Introductions: The Chairman will open the meeting, acknowledging attendees and setting the tone for the session.
2.  Apologies: A record of any members unable to attend the meeting will be noted.
3.  Declaration of Interests: Members will declare any personal or financial interests related to agenda items.
4.  Approval of Minutes: The Council will review and approve the minutes from the previous meeting, ensuring accuracy and accountability.
5.  Public Comments: A segment dedicated to public input, with the Council reserving the right to provide detailed written responses post-meeting.
6.  FY25 Budget Presentation: A comprehensive overview of the next fiscal year's budget, followed by a question and answer session.
7.  Discussion on FY25 Budget: Members will deliberate on the budget details and make recommendations as necessary.
8.  Park Renovation Project Presentation: Introduction of the proposed park renovation project, including objectives, budget, and impact, followed by a Q&A session.
9.  Discussion on Park Renovation Project: The Council will discuss the project's merits and decide on any recommendations.
10. Next Meeting Date: Setting the date and time for the next council meeting.
11. Adjournment: Official closing of the meeting, noting the end time.

**Attachments:**
-   FY25 Budget Proposal: Detailed document outlining the proposed budget for the fiscal year 2025, including revenue sources, expenditure plans, and financial forecasts.
-   Park Renovation Project Plan: Comprehensive plan for the proposed renovation of the park, detailing project scope, design, budget, and expected community benefits.
requested_output_constraints: * Cover sheet: This acts as the public notice and must include the title of the meeting, the location, date and time of the meeting, as well as the nature of the business to be discussed. It should include any information relating to legal bindings such as filming or recording the meeting and whether there is the ability to submit written representation as well as any deadlines that should be adhered to. * Agenda itself: Must be in clear English in a way a lay person can understand, formatted to 'in house' standards and government guidance, and produced in a standard font type and size as well as variabilities for disabled persons should this be required. * Associated papers: Clearly marked to correspond to agenda items, with correct titles and formatting and full information that meeds legal requirements, with confidential papers sent separately.

On first glance agendas seem simple but there is significant understanding that must go into the preparation to make sure that not only are legal requirements met but that also the papers are clear enough to encourage public engagement. Preciseness is key for clear language and short sentences. Best practices are: to prepare drafts in advance and run them by the chairman, as well as have a fresh pair of eyes look over the finished compilation to spot any errors. Common mistakes:1)  include information only items that have no need to be on the agenda to inflate the perception of the importance of the meetings and/or extend the meeting time. Only items that require a decision should be included. 2) not correctly counting clear days' notice and getting confused about bank holidays and/or weekends.

Task procedure/context:

The proposal should outline the weaknesses or flaws in the current system under the control of governments, in an attempt to ensure possible solutions with clarity, maintainability and verifiability.
